newsitem.title: USA: Carmakers clear one obstacle to cleaner U.S. cars.
newsitem.headline: Carmakers clear one obstacle to cleaner U.S. cars.

text.p: Automobile manufacturers have agreed to remove one of the main obstacles to launching a national program for cleaner cars, auto industry official said Thursday.

The American Automobile Manufacturers Association and the Association of International Automobile Manufacturers will separate their dispute with two northeastern states from the effort to introduce a cleaner car nationally.
The carmakers have been an odds with Massachusetts and New York over the states' insistence that carmakers market electric vehicles in those states to reduce air pollution.
In a letter to the Environmental Protection Agency, the carmakers said they will continue that dispute through the courts, not through the negotiations for the so-called 49-state car.

"In order to facilitate a voluntary national program, our members propose to resolve the current state ZEV (zero emission vehicle) mandate impasse through the current litigation, thereby separating this issue from the NLEV (national low emission vehicle) process," the letter said.

With that problem apparently sidestepped, the EPA may issue a proposal next week on the voluntary program to market a cleaner car in all states but California, which has stricter pollution- control measures.
"We're going to be pretty low-key when we announce it. We're not going to say there's now going to be a national LEV program," an EPA official said.

"It's not something at this point that is a very big deal. It's an important step in the process, but we're nowhere near the end of it," the official said, saying the agency must make another supplementary proposal and have a public comment period.

The EPA and other parties would have to pursue "an aggressive agenda" for the carmakers to be able to produce the cleaner cars for the 1999 model year, Jerry Esper, director of the AAMA's Vehicle Environment Department, said.

The Ozone Transport Commission, which represents northeastern states, has pushed for the national low-emissions vehicle as a way to get the necessary pollution reductions in those states to meet federal air quality standards.
